{{Infobox person|birth_date=1530|death_date={{death date|1555|12|18}}|birth_place=[[Suwa]]|gender=[[Female (gender)]]|nationality=[[Japan]]|spouse=[[Takeda Shingen]]|children=[[Takeda Katsuyori]]|father=[[Suwa Yorishige (daimyo)]]|relatives=[[Chōkyū]]}}
'''Suwa Gorōnin''' (諏訪御料人, 1530 – December 18, 1555) was a concubine of [[Takeda Shingen]]{{efn|Japanese feudal lord (1521–1573)|12=simple|13=User:Immanuelle/Takeda Shingen|ja_comment=jawiki link invalid}} (Takeda Harunobu) and the mother of [[Takeda Katsuyori|Takeda Katsuyori]]. She was the daughter of [[Suwa Yorishige|Suwa Yorishige]], the head of the [[Suwa clan|Suwa clan]], and his concubine from the [[Omi clan (麻績氏)]] (Omishi). Known also as "Taikata-sama," her actual name remains unknown. In historical sources, she is referred to as "Suwa Gorōnin" or "Suwa Gozen," both terms indicating a noblewoman.

== Biography ==
Suwa Gorōnin's birth year is uncertain, but according to the ''[[Kōyō Gunkan|Kōyō Gunkan]]'', she became a concubine of Takeda Shingen at age 14 in 1545, suggesting she was born in 1530.<ref name="hira23">{{Cite book|author=平山優|title=長篠合戦と武田勝頼 敗者の日本史9|publisher=吉川弘文館|year=2014|page=23}}</ref><ref name="shiba476">{{Cite book|author=柴辻俊六|title=武田氏家臣団人名辞典|publisher=東京堂出版|year=2015|page=476}}</ref> ''Kōyō Gunkan'' praises her beauty, calling her a "notable beauty."<ref name="shiba476" />

At the time of her father Suwa Yorishige's leadership, the Suwa clan was allied with the [[Takeda clan|Takeda clan]]. Yorishige married [[Nene Goryōnin|Neene]], Takeda Shingen's half-sister, to strengthen the alliance. However, in 1541, after Shingen ousted his father [[Takeda Nobutora|Takeda Nobutora]], Yorishige aligned with the [[Uesugi clan|Uesugi clan]], violating the Takeda-Suwa alliance. This led to Takeda's invasion of Suwa, resulting in the fall of the Suwa clan and Yorishige's forced seppuku.

To consolidate his control, Shingen took Suwa Gorōnin as a concubine and planned to have their son, Katsuyori, inherit the Suwa clan's legacy.<ref name="hira23" /> She is believed to have entered the Takeda household around 1545, residing at the [[Tsutsujigasaki Castle|Tsutsujigasaki Mansion]].<ref name="shiba476" />

Suwa Gorōnin died on November 6, 1555. Her grave is located at [[Kenpuku-ji]] in present-day [[Ina, Nagano|Ina, Nagano]]. Her Buddhist name was recorded as "Kenpukuji-dono Baigan Myōkō Daizenni."<ref name="shiba476" /> Another memorial exists at [[Kannon-in (Okaya City)]] in [[Okaya, Nagano|Okaya, Nagano]], but it was constructed after her death based on fictional accounts.

== Influence and Legacy ==
According to ''[[Tetsuzan-shū]]'' and ''Butsugan Zenji Goroku,'' her son Katsuyori performed rituals in her memory, including the 17th death anniversary ceremony in 1571.<ref name="shiba476" />

There is speculation that she was adopted by [[Netsu Motonao]] to avoid her identity as a former enemy's daughter. This adoption would mean Katsuyori and [[Takeda Nobukiyo]] were both her children, suggesting she lived until the 1560s.

== Cultural Impact ==
Suwa Gorōnin is often depicted as Takeda Shingen's favorite concubine, although this characterization is debated among historians. Historical dramas and novels have contributed to this portrayal, such as [[Jirō Nitta|Jirō Nitta]]'s ''[[Takeda Shingen (novel)]]'', where she is called "Koi-hime," and [[Yasushi Inoue|Yasushi Inoue]]'s ''[[The Samurai Banner of Furin Kazan]]'', where she is named "Yūbu-hime." 

The annual [[Shingen-ko Festival|Shingen-kō Festival]] in [[Kōfu|Kōfu, Yamanashi]] features a "Koi-hime Contest," adding to her legacy in popular culture.

== Depictions in Media ==
Suwa Gorōnin has been portrayed under various names in films and television dramas:
* ''[[Samurai Banners|Fūrin Kazan (movie)]]'' as Yūbu-hime (1969, Toho, actress: [[Yoshiko Sakuma|Yoshiko Sakuma]])
* ''[[Takeda Shingen (1988 TV series)]]'' as Koi-hime (1988, NHK Taiga Drama, actress: [[Yoko Minamino|Yōko Minamino]])
* ''[[Fūrin Kazan (TV series)|Fūrin Kazan (NHK Taiga Drama)]]'' as Yūbu-hime (2007, NHK Taiga Drama, actress: [[Yuki Shibamoto|Kō Shibamoto]])
